tagline.text: The red beach at Palo, where the promise "I have returned" was cast in bronze

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 per person (half day from Tacloban)

image.credit: U.S. Navy photo by Lt. Chuck Bell / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Gaetano Faillace (U.S. Army Signal Corps) / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A national memorial park built on Palo's Red Beach, where General MacArthur landed on
October 20, 1944
to keep his promise, "I shall return." A monumental bronze sculpture of seven figures wading ashore vividly recreates the opening scene of the liberation of the Philippines.
The Leyte Landing Memorial, formally the MacArthur Landing Memorial National Park, sits on the coast at Palo, about

south of Tacloban, the capital of Leyte Province. This beach was known during World War II by its American military codename, "Red Beach," and it's where General Douglas MacArthur stepped off a landing craft on
October 20, 1944
alongside Sergio Osmeña, president of the Philippine Commonwealth government-in-exile, wading through knee-deep seawater to shore. Having fled the Philippines for Australia in
with the vow "I shall return," MacArthur declared in a radio address that day, "I have returned."

The Leyte landing marked the start of the campaign to liberate the Philippines. It launched the Battle of Leyte, fought jointly by American, Australian, and Filipino guerrilla forces, and just days after the landing, on
October 23–26
, one of history's largest naval engagements, the Battle of Leyte Gulf, dealt a decisive blow to the Japanese navy. On
October 23
, the Commonwealth government of the Philippines was restored in Tacloban, and the city briefly served as a temporary capital.
The park covers about
and was designated a national park in

. Its centerpiece is a group of seven bronze statues by sculptor Anastacio Caedo, standing about twice life-size in a shallow artificial pool. Their composition faithfully recreates the famous landing photograph taken by combat photographer Gaetano Faillace, showing MacArthur and Osmeña alongside Lieutenant General Sutherland, Brigadier General Romulo, Major General Whitney, Sergeant Salveron, and CBS correspondent William Dunn. The statues were unveiled in
, on the 37th anniversary of the landing.
In
, Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) toppled the Romulo statue, but it was quickly restored, and every year on
October 20

, an anniversary ceremony marking the Leyte Gulf landing is still held here. The sights themselves take only an hour or two, but for travelers interested in war history, or families visiting Tacloban, it's a rewarding half-day stop combined with the San Juanico Bridge and Tacloban's other wartime landmarks.

blocks.title: Photos Before the Seven Bronze Figures

children.text: The statues wade ashore with their backs to the sea, so a slightly angled shot captures all seven figures better than a straight-on one. Morning light, which falls on the front of the statues, photographs more brightly than the afternoon, when the sun is behind them.

blocks.title: Comparing the Statues to the 1944 Landing Photo

children.text: Pull up Faillace's original landing photograph on your phone and compare it side by side with the statues. The figures' poses and order match the photo almost exactly, giving a real sense of stepping into a moment of history.

blocks.title: Touring the Garden of Peace Stones

children.text: Built for the 50th anniversary of the landing in
, this garden displays stones sent by leaders of participating nations and other countries as tokens of peace. It's worth a slow walk along the path behind the statues.

blocks.title: Reading the Historical Marker and MacArthur's Proclamation

children.text: A marker from the National Historical Commission stands nearby, along with a bronze plaque of MacArthur's landing proclamation, which begins "To the People of the Philippines." Written in both English and Filipino, it's a concise summary of the events of the time.

The wide waters of Leyte Gulf open up in front of the statues. Part of this site's charm is walking the beach the troops came ashore on, looking out toward Samar Island on the horizon and the fishing boats passing by.
The ceremony held every
October 20
draws veterans and diplomats from the U.S., Australia, Japan, and other countries, and in some years includes a reenactment of the landing. Leyte Province designates this day a special local holiday.
About
10 minutes
by car away are Palo Metropolitan Cathedral, used as a U.S. field hospital during the Battle of Leyte, and Guinhandang Hill (Hill 522), a battle site topped with a cross at the end of 522 steps.
The mansion MacArthur used as his headquarters after the landing served briefly as the seat of the provisional government in
October 1944
. It's now used for other purposes and interior visits are limited, but you can still view the exterior and marker.

Tacloban's war landmarks are close together, so getting around by taxi or a chartered tricycle is efficient. Hours at the bridge and museum can change, so check the day before.

During weight-limit periods on the San Juanico Bridge, large buses have sometimes had passengers transfer before crossing, so confirm the current arrangement before departing.

Eastern Visayas faces the Pacific and sees considerable rain.
March–June
, when skies are relatively clear and the sea calm, is the best time to visit, while
November–January
brings frequent overcast and rainy days from the northeast monsoon.
July–December
often falls in typhoon season, so check the forecast closely.
The park sits on a shade-poor coastline, so it gets the full brunt of the sun at midday, around
or after
4 PM
is better for walking. Around
October 20

each year, the landing anniversary ceremony and related events bring plenty to see, though the area around the statues may be restricted during the ceremony itself. Timing your trip around Tacloban's Pintados-Kasadyaan Festival in late
June
is another good option.

children.text: Prices are rough estimates as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Downtown Tacloban, with its concentration of restaurants and transport, is the most convenient base. Small hotels in the city center run about
a night, while mid-range hotels around the coastal road toward the airport and the shopping malls run about
. Right next to the memorial, a beachfront resort-style hotel suits travelers who want a quiet stay overlooking Leyte Gulf (about
a night).

In the afternoon, stalls selling snacks and drinks set up around the memorial, but for a proper meal, it's better to eat in Palo town or Tacloban. Leyte's signature snacks are binagol, made from taro and coconut, and moron, glutinous rice twisted with chocolate and steamed in banana leaf. Being a coastal city, there are plenty of restaurants serving grilled fish, squid, and kinilaw (vinegar-cured raw fish), and the evening seafront stalls in Tacloban offer cheap barbecue skewers.
Entry to the park is free, with no ticket booth. Signs sometimes restrict bringing food and drinks inside, so eat any snacks outside.
The sights take only
1–2 hours
, so it's efficient to plan a route combining Palo Cathedral, Guinhandang Hill, and San Juanico Bridge.
Photograph the statues in the morning, when the light falls on their front and there's no backlighting. A wide-angle lens helps fit all seven figures and the sea into one frame.
Looking up Faillace's 1944 landing photo and MacArthur's "I have returned" speech before your visit makes the site feel much more vivid.
There's almost no shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen, and water — it's easiest to buy these at a convenience store in Palo town beforehand.
During the October ceremony, expect traffic control and crowds — arrive early in the morning if you want to see the event, or choose a date before or after it for a quieter visit.
Downtown Tacloban has plenty of ATMs and malls, but tricycles and street stalls take cash only, so bring small bills.
The park was heavily upgraded in
and in
, the 80th anniversary of the landing, gaining an observation deck, an amphitheater, a visitor center, a musical fountain, and a lagoon, and free public Wi-Fi was also installed in
July 2025
. Check on-site whether facilities are operating.

Climbing onto the pool or pedestal where the statues stand, or posing while holding onto a statue, is prohibited. This is a memorial space honoring war casualties, so please view it quietly and respectfully.
The beach isn't maintained for swimming and can have waves and currents, so it's safer to avoid going in the water.
During typhoon season (
July–December
), flight cancellations and flooded roads can occur, so build a day of slack into your itinerary.
Park access may be restricted on days with a ceremony or an official visit, so check local government notices.
The strong midday sun poses a heatstroke risk. If traveling with children or older family members, visit in the morning or late afternoon.
Mosquitoes are common in the rainy season, raising the risk of dengue fever. Bring insect repellent.
